passages.title: By the pen: you are not possessed
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing.** The people of Makkah had run out of arguments against the Prophet ﷺ, so they fell back on an insult: *he is mad*. These seven ayat are Allah's answer to that slander. He opens with an oath — by the pen and by what is written with it — and then, in one unbroken movement, denies the charge (ayah 2), points to the unending reward the Prophet ﷺ has earned (ayah 3), declares his character sublime (ayah 4), promises that time itself will reveal who was really out of his mind (ayat 5–6), and closes by placing the whole verdict in the hands of the One who alone knows who is astray and who is guided (ayah 7). It is a defence of the Messenger ﷺ, delivered by his Lord.

## The setting: why they said "majnūn"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the thread from the previous sūrah. Sūrat al-Mulk established the existence of Allah, His Oneness, His knowledge and power, arguing from His creation of death and life and the beautiful order running through the cosmos — and it noted how ungrateful man has repeatedly rejected the Divine message. Sūrat al-Qalam takes the next step: it establishes the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ own claim, and answers the taunts thrown at him.

Their first and favourite taunt was madness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests several reasons why they reached for that word:

- **The state of revelation.** When an instalment of revelation came down on him ﷺ, a physical change would come over him — the colour of his face would change and redden, sometimes he would snore, sometimes he seemed weighed down with grief, sometimes he would hang his head. When the state passed he would recite the revealed verses to the people. This was entirely outside their experience, so they filed it under insanity.
- **The message itself.** He told his people — and the whole world — that nothing deserves worship except Allah, and that their hand-carved idols cannot be gods, because they are insensate, without knowledge, and unable to benefit or harm anyone.
- **The sheer loneliness of it.** His was a single voice of truth, with no apparent means and no visible support, standing unwaveringly against the entire world. People with no insight or foresight could not imagine him ever reaching his goal, so they called the attempt madness.
- **And some**, Maʿārif adds bluntly, called him insane simply for the sake of calling him insane, with no reason at all. Having no way to refute what he taught, the slur was all they had left.

The opening ayat of the sūrah refute that charge — and they do it under an emphatic oath.

## Nūn

The sūrah opens with a single letter: **Nūn**. Ibn Kathir treats it exactly as he treats **Ṣād** at the head of Sūrah 38 and **Qāf**, and the other disconnected letters that open various sūrahs — he refers the reader back to his long discussion at the start of Sūrat al-Baqarah and does not repeat it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more explicit: these isolated letters are among the secret signs and symbols and mysteries of Allah. Allah alone knows their hidden meaning — or He made their meaning known to His Messenger ﷺ — and the Ummah is not permitted to go digging for it. That restraint is itself a lesson: not everything in the Book is given to us to unlock.

## "By the pen"

In *wa-l-qalam*, the **wāw** is the particle of oath — hence "by the pen." Allah swears by an instrument so ordinary we barely notice it.

**Which pen?** Ibn Kathir says the apparent meaning is the actual pen people write with, and he links it to the very first revelation: "Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous. Who has taught by the pen. He has taught man that which he knew not" (96:3–5). On that reading, Allah is swearing by the pen in order to wake His creatures up to a favour they take for granted — that He taught them the skill of writing, through which knowledge is attained. Qatadah likewise called the pen a great gift Allah bestowed on His servants.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three kinds of pen: the pen of destinies, the pen of the angels, and the pen of human beings — and the oath may take in any or all of them. Abu Ḥātim al-Busti defined *qalam* simply as an object used for writing anything. Ibn ʿAbbās held that here it means specifically **the pen of destinies**. Some scholars harmonise the two: Allah first created the pen of decrees, which recorded the destinies of the whole universe and every creature, and then created the second pen, the one used by the inhabitants of the earth — the pen of 96:4, "He taught by the pen." And Allah knows best.

**"And what they write"** (*wa mā yasṭurūn*). Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah all explained this as "what they write." As-Suddī said it means the angels and the deeds of the servants which they record — so the oath sweeps in the register kept over every human life.

**The Pen of decree.** Those who read *al-qalam* as the pen of destiny cite hadiths about it. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Walīd ibn ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit that his father called him as he lay dying and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *Verily, the first of what Allah created was the Pen, and He said to it: 'Write.' The Pen said: 'O my Lord, what shall I write?' He said: 'Write the decree and whatever will be throughout eternity.'*" Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad recorded it through various routes, and that at-Tirmidhi recorded it and said of it, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ, Gharīb." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah recorded the destiny of all creatures 50,000 years before creating the heavens and the earth" — in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**.

**Why swear by a pen at all?** If it is the pen of destinies, Maʿārif notes, its greatness needs no explaining. If it is pens in general — the decree's pen, the angels' pens, and ours — the oath is still perfectly apt, because all great tasks are accomplished by the pen; even in the conquest of territories the pen plays a mighty role. Abu Ḥātim al-Busti put it in two lines of verse, which run in sense: when brave men swear by their swords and count the sword among the things that bring men honour, the writer's pen is honour and elevation enough for all time — because Allah Himself swore an oath by the pen.

## The logic of a Qur'anic oath

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags a principle worth carrying to every oath in the Qur'an: **whenever Allah swears by something, that thing is itself cited as evidence for the claim being made.** The oath is not decoration; it is exhibit A.

So here, "what they write" is the proof of the denial that follows. The written record of the world — history itself — is placed before the critics. Let them turn its pages and find, if they can, one man of this calibre, of these morals, who was insane. As Maʿārif puts it: he is the one who takes care of other people's sanity.

## Ayah 2: "By the grace of your Lord, you are not insane"

Ibn Kathir paraphrases: *you are not crazy, as the ignorant among your people claim* — and all praise is due to Allah. Those who say it are the ones denying the guidance and the clear truth he brought; it is precisely because of that guidance that they pin madness on him.

Notice the phrase **bi-niʿmati rabbik**, "by the grace of your Lord." Maʿārif points out that the ayah does not merely state the claim; it supplies the evidence in the same breath. A man on whom Allah has conferred such blessing and grace cannot possibly be insane. Turn the pages of history and see. And then the tafsir turns the accusation round on the accusers: **calling such a sane man insane is itself insanity.**

There is tenderness in the wording too: Allah does not leave the denial flat, but attaches it to His own favour upon His Messenger ﷺ. The refutation is itself a gift.

## Ayah 3: a reward that is never cut off

"And verily, for you will be a reward that is not *mamnūn*." Ibn Kathir explains: a great reward and abundant blessings that will never be cut off or perish — earned because he conveyed his Lord's message to creation and bore their abuse with patience. *Ghayr mamnūn* means it will not be cut off, like Allah's words "a gift without an end" (11:108) and "then they shall have a reward without end" (95:6). Mujāhid glossed it as "without reckoning" — a reward not measured out and counted, which comes back to the same generosity.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows how this ayah keeps hammering the same nail: the actions of a madman produce no useful result, and no insane person is ever rewarded for his actions. Yet this man ﷺ would eminently succeed in the object of his Divine mission and bring about a wonderful revolution in the lives of a degenerate and demented people. A never-ending reward is the mark of a life that achieved something — the opposite of the charge.

Note the order: the insult is denied in ayah 2, and before any argument about his character is made, ayah 3 tells him what he is receiving. Whatever they say, his account with his Lord is secure and inexhaustible.

## Ayah 4: "You are truly of outstanding character"

This is the crown of the passage, and the sources give it the most room. Maʿārif frames it as an invitation to the very people making the accusation: think carefully about the lofty morals of this man ﷺ.

**What the early authorities said.** Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of al-ʿAwfī, said: "Verily, you are on a great religion, and it is Islam" — and Ibn Kathir notes that Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, as-Suddī, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd all said the same. ʿAlī said it signifies the good manners the Qur'an has taught. And ʿĀʾishah, asked about the character of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by Saʿd ibn Hishām, answered: "Have you not read the Qur'an?" He said, "Of course." She said: **"Verily, the character of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the Qur'an."** Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Muslim recorded this in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from Qatādah, in full. Maʿārif observes that all these interpretations come to almost the same thing: he ﷺ is the living example of the Qur'an that teaches high morals.

Ibn Kathir unpacks ʿĀʾishah's answer: he ﷺ acted by the commands and prohibitions of the Qur'an. His nature and character were patterned on it — whatever the Qur'an commanded he did, whatever it forbade he avoided, setting aside the pull of his own disposition. Alongside that, Allah gave him the exalted character: modesty, kindness, bravery, readiness to pardon, gentleness, and every other good quality.

**What those who lived with him saw.** Anas said — confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs — "I served the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for ten years, and he never said a word of displeasure to me (*uff*), nor did he ever say about something I had done, 'Why did you do that?', nor about something I had not done, 'Why didn't you do this?' He had the best character; I never touched silk or anything softer than the palm of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and I never smelled any musk or perfume with a better fragrance than his." Maʿārif adds the obvious: ten years is a long time, long enough for something unpleasant or objectionable to have happened.

Al-Barāʾ said — recorded by Imam al-Bukhārī — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had the most handsome face of all people and the best behaviour of all people, and that he was neither tall nor short.

ʿĀʾishah said, in a narration Ibn Kathir attributes to Imam Ahmad and Maʿārif to Muslim, that he ﷺ never struck a servant with his hand, nor a woman, nor struck anything with his hand except when fighting in the cause of Allah; that he never avenged himself for harm done to him, and only implemented Allah's punishment on those who violated Allah's limits. Ibn Kathir's wording adds that whenever he ﷺ was given a choice between two things he chose the easier of them, so long as it was no sin — and if it involved sin, no one kept farther from it than he did.

Jābir said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was never asked for anything and answered "no" — in Bukhārī and Muslim. ʿĀʾishah said he was never vulgar, never pretended to be, never shouted in the marketplaces, and never responded to evil with evil but always pardoned and overlooked. And Anas related that, such was his noble character, any slave-girl of Madinah could take him by the hand and lead him wherever she wished. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that the narratives it cites in this section are taken from Tafsīr Maẓharī; these last two it relays without naming a collection.)

Ibn Kathir remarks that the hadiths on this subject are numerous, and points the reader to Abū ʿĪsā at-Tirmidhi's whole book on it, *Kitāb ash-Shamāʾil*.

**The mission itself was character.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"I have only been sent to perfect righteous behavior."** Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in recording it; Maʿārif cites a near-identical wording — "I have only been sent to perfect noble character" — from Abū Ḥayyān.

**And what it weighs.** Abū ad-Dardāʾ narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that noble character will be the heaviest thing on a Muslim's scale of good deeds on the Day of Resurrection, and that Allah detests the rude and foul-mouthed person — transmitted by at-Tirmidhī, who graded it *ḥasan*. ʿĀʾishah narrated that by virtue of good character a believer can attain the status of those who spend their nights in worship and their days fasting — Abū Dāwūd. And when Muʿādh ibn Jabal put his foot in the stirrup, departing as governor of Yemen, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ advised him: *"O Muʿādh, display your best character with people"* — transmitted by Mālik.

Read together, ayah 4 does two things at once: it demolishes the slander, and it hands the believer the standard to live by.

## Ayat 5–6: "You will see, and they will see"

"So you will see, and they will see — which of you is *maftūn*." Ibn Kathir: it means *you will know, O Muhammad, and those who oppose and reject you will know, who is insane and misguided among you.* He sets it beside "Tomorrow they will come to know who is the liar, the insolent one!" (54:26) and "And verily, either we or you are rightly guided or in plain error" (34:24) — the calm confidence of truth that does not need to shout.

Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that *maftūn* here means the one who is crazy, and Mujāhid and others said the same; Maʿārif renders it "demented." Ibn Kathir adds that the literal meaning of *maftūn* is one who has been **charmed or lured away from the truth and has strayed from it** — a person under a spell, pulled off course. That is a sharper picture than mere madness: the real derangement is being seduced away from what is plainly true. Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the knowing referred to here is on the Day of Judgement.

Maʿārif hears a prophecy in it, and a turning of the tables: told in challenging words, time will show whether it was he or they who suffered from insanity — whether his claim to be Allah's Messenger ﷺ was the outpouring of a heated brain, or whether they were the deranged ones, unable to read the signs of their time. Those who never saw the light of truth were disgraced and defeated in this world. But thousands of others who at first did not see it and denounced him as demented soon saw the light and embraced Islam, taking love and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ as the capital asset of their success, prosperity and happiness. The ayah left the door open — and many walked through it.

## Ayah 7: the verdict belongs to Allah

"Verily, your Lord is the best Knower of him who has gone astray from His path, and He is the best Knower of those who are guided." Ibn Kathir: He knows which of the two groups among you is truly guided, and He knows the party that is astray from the truth.

This is where the passage rests. The argument is not settled by whoever shouts loudest or whichever side is currently larger; it is settled by the knowledge of Allah, which encompasses both the strayed and the guided exactly as they are. Notice that guidance and misguidance are described here as knowledge belonging to your **Lord** — *rabbaka* — picking up the *rabbik* of ayah 2, "by the grace of your Lord." The Prophet ﷺ is being told, in effect: the One whose grace shields you from their slander is also the One who keeps the true record of everyone in this dispute.

## Living it

- **Honour the pen.** Allah swore by it. Writing is how knowledge is attained; treat what you write, and what you read, as something Allah found worthy of an oath.
- **Take the decree seriously.** The Pen was told to write the decree and whatever will be throughout eternity — recorded, as the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim says, fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth. That is a settled matter to rest in, not a puzzle to solve.
- **Character is the argument.** When the Prophet ﷺ was slandered, Allah's defence of him was his conduct. Noble character will be the heaviest thing on a Muslim's scale on the Day of Resurrection.
- **Absorb insult without retaliating.** He ﷺ never avenged himself for harm done to him; he acted only where the limits of Allah were violated.
- **Leave the verdict to Allah.** You are not required to prove your own vindication. "You will see, and they will see" — and your Lord already knows.

passages.title: Do not yield to the slanderous rich denier
passages.tafsir:
Ibn Kathir gives this passage a heading that states its subject exactly: "Prohibition of giving in to the Pressure of the Disbelievers and Their Suggestions, and that They like to meet in the Middle of the Path." Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ not to give in — and then paints a portrait of the kind of man whose lead is not worth following, so devastating that the Prophet ﷺ could never mistake him for someone worth pleasing.

What holds ayat 8–16 together is a single command repeated twice — *do not obey* — first about a group (the deniers, ayah 8), then about one individual described in merciless detail (ayat 10–13). The rest of the passage explains why that individual carried such weight (his wealth and children, ayah 14), how he responded to it (ayah 15), and what Allah will do to him in the end (ayah 16).

## The wish, and why it is refused (8–9)

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 8 as flowing directly out of what came just before it. Allah has favoured His Messenger ﷺ, and the sense is: *just as We have favoured you and given you the upright legislation and great character* — **so do not obey the deniers**.

That is the logic worth pausing over. The refusal is not built on hostility. It is built on the fact that what the Prophet ﷺ already has is a favour from Allah. You do not trade away a gift like that for the goodwill of people who reject it.

Ayah 9 exposes what they wished for: **They wish that you should compromise with them, so they (too) would compromise with you.** Ibn ʿAbbās explained it plainly: "That you would permit them (their idolatry) and they also would permit you (to practice your religion)." Mujāhid put the same thing more sharply: "This means that you should be quiet about their gods and abandon the truth that you are upon."

Notice the two halves of Mujāhid's gloss. There is a *silence* — say nothing about their gods — and there is an *abandonment* — leave the truth you are standing on. The first sounds small. The second is what the first actually costs. And Allah names the whole transaction for what it is: obedience to the deniers.

**The ruling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the rendering it adopts — *they wish that you become flexible in your faith, and they will become flexible in their hostile attitude* — rests on the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by Qurṭubī. It then draws the legal conclusion, citing Mazharī: this ayah shows that any such compromise with the unbelievers amounts to *mudāhanah fid-dīn* — flexibility, or a softening, in the religion itself — and that this is forbidden. Such a pact of leniency in matters of religion is not permissible, unless one is compelled by necessity.

The exception matters as much as the rule. What the ruling closes off is the *bargain*: a pact of leniency in matters of religion. And it keeps open the case of the one who is genuinely compelled.

## The portrait: fault upon fault (10–13)

Ayah 10 narrows from the group to a type: **And do not obey every ḥallāf mahīn.**

- **Ḥallāf** — one who swears oaths constantly. Ibn Kathir explains *why* such a man does this: a liar, because of his weakness and his disgracefulness, can find no protection except in his false oaths, which he swears boldly using Allah's Names — all the time, and out of place, where no oath was called for. The swearing is the symptom; the emptiness underneath is the disease. A man whose word carries weight does not need to keep invoking Allah to be believed.
- **Mahīn** — Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Al-Mahin means the liar." Ibn Kathir's own rendering of the word carries both senses, "liar or worthless person," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān translates it "contemptible." Hold that against ayah 14: this is a man of wealth and children, and Allah's verdict on him is *mahīn*.

Ayah 11 turns to what he does with his tongue: **hammāz, mashshāʾ bi-namīm.**

- **Hammāz** — Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah both said: "This is slander."
- **Mashshāʾ bi-namīm** — Ibn Kathir describes the one who goes around among people instigating discord between them and carrying tales, *in order to* corrupt relations between people **when they are good and pleasant**. Two things in that gloss are worth slowing down for. The purpose clause — *in order to* — makes this deliberate, not careless. And the closing phrase is the sting: this is not someone mishandling a quarrel that already existed. The relationships he works on are the intact ones.

### From the Sunnah on namīmah

Ibn Kathir brings two hadith here, and they land heavily on a sin many people treat as ordinary conversation.

It is confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Mujāhid from Ṭāwūs from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once passed by two graves and said: *"Verily, these two are being punished, and they are not being punished for something major. One of them was not careful about protecting himself from urine. The other one used to spread namīmah."* Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has been recorded by the Group in their books, through routes of transmission that are all on the authority of Mujāhid.

Imam Ahmad recorded that Ḥudhayfah said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying, *"The slanderer will not enter into Paradise."* Ibn Kathir says this hadith has been reported by the Group except for Ibn Mājah.

Read them together. The first says the punishment is already underway for something not counted as major. The second says where the habit ends. So when this passage asks a believer to look hard at an impressive man, the first thing it makes him look at is that man's tongue.

Ayah 12 moves to his hands and his conduct: **mannāʿ lil-khayr, muʿtad, athīm.**

- **Mannāʿ lil-khayr** — Ibn Kathir: he refuses to give, and withholds that which he has of good. A man of means whose wealth never moves outward.
- **Muʿtad** — in attaining what Allah has actually made permissible for him, he still exceeds the legislated bounds. Even the permitted is not enough for him.
- **Athīm** — and beyond that, says Ibn Kathir, he delves into the forbidden things.

There is a sequence in those three words: tight-fisted with the good he holds, then greedy past the limit within the lawful, and finally at home in the unlawful.

Ayah 13 delivers the last two strokes: **ʿutull, baʿda dhālika zanīm.**

**ʿUtull**, says Ibn Kathir, means one who is cruel, harsh, strong, greedy and stingy — physical force joined to hardness of heart.

Here Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ḥārithah ibn Wahb, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Shall I inform you of the people of Paradise? (They will be) every weak and oppressed person. When he swears by Allah, he fulfils his oath. Shall I inform you of the people of the Fire? Every ʿutull, jawwāẓ and arrogant person."* Al-Wākiʿ said, "It (ʿutull) is every jawwāẓ, jaʿẓarī and arrogant person." Ibn Kathir records that both al-Bukhārī and Muslim have it in their Two Ṣaḥīḥs, as well as the rest of the Group except for Abū Dāwūd, all its routes of transmission being by way of Sufyān ath-Thawrī and Shuʿbah, who both reported it from Saʿīd ibn Khālid. The scholars of the Arabic language, he adds, have said that *jaʿẓarī* means rude and harsh, while *jawwāẓ* means greedy and stingy.

That hadith is a mirror of these ayat. The man Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ not to obey is described by the very word the Prophet ﷺ used for the people of the Fire — *ʿutull*. And its opposite is not the powerful believer but the *weak and oppressed* one, whose distinction is that when he swears by Allah, the oath is honoured. Set him beside the *ḥallāf* of ayah 10, forever swearing and never true. Two men, two oaths, two destinations.

## Zanīm — the hardest word in the passage

**Zanīm** comes "after all that" (*baʿda dhālika*) — as though the list were already complete and one thing still remained to be said. The commentators give it more than one sense, and it is worth reporting them as they stand.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said about this ayah that he was "a man from the Quraysh who stands out among them like the sheep that has had a piece of its ear cut off." Ibn Kathir explains the image: the meaning is that he is *famous for his evil*, just as a sheep with a piece of its ear cut off stands out among its sister sheep. Everyone knows exactly who he is.

Ibn Kathir then adds a linguistic sense: in the Arabic language a *zanīm* is a person who is adopted among a group of people — that is, he is not truly of them. He attributes this to Ibn Jarīr and others among the Imams.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the word in a further direction: it refers to "a person whose legitimate birth from a father is not proved," and the person referred to in this ayah was of doubtful birth, his lineage uncertain. The English rendering carried with this passage follows that sense: *brute, and — on top of all that — an illegitimate child.*

Two things are worth holding onto. First, notice where the different senses fall. Most of ayat 10–13 is a list of chosen behaviours — lying, slander, stinginess, transgression, cruelty — and Ibn ʿAbbās's reading keeps the final word in that register too: the man is *notorious for his evil*. The other reported senses turn instead on where he stands among his people. Second, whichever sense one takes, the placement does the same work: it comes *after all that*, when the reader thinks the indictment is finished, and it strips the last thing the man could still have been trading on.

**Who was he?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: the preceding ayah prohibited any compromise with the unbelievers in general in matters of religion, while ayat 10–13 prohibit specifically yielding to such a mean leader of falsehood as Walīd ibn Mughīrah, "the worst mischief-maker," who possessed the base characteristics listed in these ayat — as transmitted by Ibn Jarīr on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn Kathir, in what is quoted here, does not name him, saying only "a man from the Quraysh." But he does set beside this passage the ayat of Sūrah al-Muddaththir (74:11–30) about the man Allah created alone, then granted resources in abundance and children to be by his side and a life made smooth and comfortable, who after all that still desired more — and who, having thought and plotted, then frowned and looked in a bad tempered way, then turned back and was proud, and said: "This is nothing but magic from that of old, this is nothing but the word of a human being!"

## Wealth as the engine of denial (14–15)

Ayah 14 names the cause: **because he had wealth and children.** Ibn Kathir reads it as an indictment of ingratitude — *this* is how he responds to the favours that Allah has bestowed upon him of wealth and children: by disbelieving in Allah's ayat and turning away from them.

Ayah 15 shows the form the turning away takes. **When Our ayat are recited to him, he says: "Tales of the men of old!"** He does not argue. He does not weigh the claim. He reaches for a dismissal — *asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, the tales of the men of old — claiming, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that they are a lie that has been taken from the tales of the ancients.

Read the two ayat as Ibn Kathir joins them, and the causal link is startling: the very favours that should have produced gratitude are what produced the dismissal. Wealth and children were the gift; disbelief and turning away are what he returned for them.

These two ayat also explain the passage backwards. Why would anyone defer to the man of ayat 10–13? Not for his character — that has just been catalogued fault by fault. The reason ayah 14 gives is wealth and children. The passage prises apart a man's *weight* among people and his *worth* before Allah, and it does so permanently.

## The branding (16)

**We shall brand him on the khurṭūm.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that his nose has been described this way *by way of reproach*: *khurṭūm* refers specifically to the long nose of a pig or the trunk of an elephant. It is the vocabulary of the animal pen, chosen deliberately as a rebuke.

Ibn Kathir preserves two readings of the branding:

- **Ibn Jarīr:** "We will make his matter clear and evident so that they will know him and he will not be hidden from them, just as the branding mark on the snouts (of animals)." His disgrace becomes public and unmistakable, the way a brand is.
- **Others:** this is the mark of the people of the Hellfire — meaning, *We will blacken his face on the Day of Judgement* — and the face has been referred to here as a snout.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān joins the two ideas and names the motive being answered: because the disbelievers, out of pride and a false sense of power, rejected the Divine Message in this world, Allah will disgrace and humiliate them on the Day of Resurrection, so that the earlier and later generations will be able to see it.

That is the shape of the whole passage in one ayah. The pride that refused the message in this world is met by a disgrace that the earlier and later generations will witness — and the man whose lead the Prophet ﷺ was told not to follow is himself marked before all creation.

## Living it

- **Recognise the bargain for what it is.** The ruling in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise: a pact of leniency in matters of religion is *mudāhanah fid-dīn* and is not permissible, unless one is compelled by necessity. Mujāhid's gloss shows how such a bargain works — a silence about their gods on one side, and the abandoning of the truth you stand on as the real price.
- **Weigh people by character, not by clout.** This whole passage exists because a man's lead was worth warning against. Ayah 14 names wealth and children as what stood behind him — after ayat 10–13 have already shown what he actually was.
- **Take namīmah seriously.** The Prophet ﷺ said of the two in the graves that they were "not being punished for something major," and yet they were being punished; and the slanderer, he said, will not enter into Paradise. Carrying tales — especially, in Ibn Kathir's words, where relations between people are good and pleasant — is exactly the trait Allah lists among the marks of a man not to be obeyed.
- **Watch your oaths.** Constant swearing by Allah's Names, all the time and out of place, is presented here as the refuge of someone with no other protection for his word. The person of Paradise in the hadith is the one who, when he swears by Allah, fulfils his oath.
- **Let the favour of Allah steady you.** The command in ayah 8 rests on what precedes it: the upright legislation and the great character Allah gave His Messenger ﷺ. Someone who knows what Allah has given him does not need approval badly enough to sell any part of it.

passages.title: The garden owners swear, and the garden burns
passages.tafsir:
Allah tells a story here — a story about a family who inherited a beautiful garden, resolved one night to cut the poor out of its harvest, and woke to find that Allah had cut them out of it instead. Ayat 17–25 carry the story from the whispered oath to the moment the brothers march out at dawn, still confident, not yet knowing that everything they are walking towards is already ash.

What holds these nine ayat together is a single night and the morning that follows it: a plan made in the dark (17–18), a silent visitation while the planners slept (19–20), and a brisk, self-satisfied departure at first light (21–25). The reader is told what happened to the garden in ayah 20; the owners are not told until ayah 26. We watch them hurry towards a ruin they cannot see.

## Why this story, and why here

The verses just before this passage answered the criticisms the pagan Arabs were levelling against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Now, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the Qurʼan turns from rebuttal to warning: it tells a story of the past, and the unbelievers of Makkah are threatened with punishment.

Ibn Kathir states the comparison plainly. This is a parable Allah made of the behaviour of the Quraysh disbelievers with the great mercy and the tremendous favours He granted them — above all the mercy and favour of sending Muhammad ﷺ to them — which they met with denial, rejection and opposition. The garden owners had wealth handed to them by a righteous father and treated it as theirs to hoard; Makkah had a Prophet ﷺ sent to it and met him with rejection. In both cases the gift itself is the test, and in both cases the gift can be taken away in a night.

That is the force of the opening words in ayah 17: **إِنَّا بَلَوْنَاهُمْ** — "Indeed We have tested them." Ibn Kathir glosses *balawnā* simply: "We have tested them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this "testing" may point forward to the story itself — people blessed with divine favours who behaved ungratefully, so that a punishment came upon them and the favours were destroyed. Read that way, the Makkans' own flourishing businesses and prosperity, and above all the coming of the Messenger ﷺ, were the examination paper: would they behave gratefully to Allah and believe in Him and His Messenger ﷺ, or obstinately persist in disbelief?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this interpretation holds even if these verses are taken as Makkan, but that most commentators take them to be Madani. On that reading the "test" is a specific one: the terrible famine that held Makkah in its grip, as a result of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer against them, for several years — years in which people died of hunger and starvation and were forced to eat carrion and the leaves of trees, until the Makkans begged the Prophet ﷺ to pray for their deliverance from the scourge. This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, took place after the migration. Either way the lesson stands: a people who answer blessing with ingratitude should draw a lesson from the story of the owners of the orchard, lest they be visited by a similar punishment.

## The family and the garden

Both commentaries preserve the background, and it is worth having in full, because the story only bites once you know who these men were.

Ibn Kathir reports that some of the Salaf — the earliest generations of Muslims — mentioned that these people were from Yemen, and that Saʿid bin Jubayr said they were from a village called Darawan, six miles from Sanʿaʼ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the same account from elders such as Ibn ʿAbbas, giving the distance as about two farsakhs (six miles), and traces the report to the narration of Muhammad Ibn Marwan on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also been said, Ibn Kathir records, that they were from the people of Ethiopia; and both commentaries note that they were from the People of the Book. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qurtubi that the incident took place a while after the Ascension of Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon him). The scholars differed on the location; the Qurʼan itself does not name it, and Allah knows best.

The garden was set up by a pious and righteous man. Ibn Kathir describes how he handled it: whatever he reaped from it he would put back into the garden as it needed, he would save some of it as food for his dependants for the year, and he would give away the excess in charity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the texture. When he picked the fruit or harvested the crop with the sickle, he would give some of the crop to the poor and indigent who gathered grain for themselves. When the crop was threshed and the grain separated from the chaff, he would leave the grain for the poor. When fruits were picked from the trees and some fell to the ground, he left them for the indigent. For this reason, the poor always gathered at the orchard at the time of picking the fruit and separating the grain. They knew when to come. It was, in effect, a standing appointment between the rich and the poor of that place.

Then he died, and three sons inherited the orchard and the crop-fields. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports their family meeting: the family had grown large, the produce of the orchard and land was not sufficient for them, and so it was no longer possible to spare any fruit or grain for the poor. According to other narratives, it says, these boys — like other youngsters — felt that their father had been a fool to give away so much, and thought it necessary to put a stop to it. Ibn Kathir preserves the same verdict in their own mouths: "Verily, our father was foolish for giving some of this garden's harvest to the poor. If we prevent them from it, then we will have more."

That sentence is the hinge of the whole passage. They did not deny Allah. They simply re-classified generosity as waste.

## The oath, and the words that were not said

**"When they swore to pluck its fruits in the morning" (17).** Ibn Kathir explains that they vowed between themselves during the night that they would pluck the fruit of the garden in the morning, so that the poor and the beggars would not know what they were doing — in this way they would be able to keep its fruit for themselves and not give any of it in charity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more precise still: they swore that they would harvest very early in the morning and return with it before the throng of poor people could arrive at the garden. Note what the plan actually is. It is not a refusal — it is a schedule. They will simply arrive before the poor do.

**"And they made no exception" (18).** The Arabic is **وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the term *istithnāʼ*: it means "to make an exception by saying *inshaʼAllah*" — "if Allah wills." So the men swore an unqualified oath about tomorrow with no reference to the will of the One who owns tomorrow. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling straight out of it: it is *sunnah* — the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, the way he taught his community to speak and act — to say *inshaʼAllah* when one mentions that one will do a particular work tomorrow. These men had so much confidence in their plan that they did not say the redeeming words.

Ibn Kathir's comment is chilling in its brevity: this was the vow they made without saying "if Allah wills" — "therefore, Allah broke their vow."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a second reading of the same phrase, from Mazhari: that some scholars interpret it here to mean that they would devour the entire harvest themselves, with no exception for the poor. Both senses fit the story exactly — no exception made for Allah's will, and no exception made for Allah's poor. The two failures are one failure.

## What came in the night

**"Then there passed over it a ṭāʼif from your Lord while they slept" (19).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the word as a "whirl" — a whirl of calamity — as a result of which the divine punishment overtook the garden in a sudden and swift sweep. Ibn Kathir glosses it: it was afflicted with some heavenly destruction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some narratives report it was a fire, which burnt every standing crop and reduced it to black ashes.

Two things in the wording of ayah 19 deserve attention.

First, **مِّن رَّبِّكَ** — "from *your* Lord." The narrative turns for a moment and addresses its hearer directly. The men in the garden never see a hand; the one being told the story is told exactly whose hand it was.

Second, **وَهُمْ نَائِمُونَ** — "while they were asleep." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses it: the devastating disaster overtook the entire garden while its owners were asleep. They had spent the night engineering the perfect early start, and the night was precisely when they lost everything. The clock they were racing had already run out.

**"So by the morning it was like aṣ-ṣarīm" (20).** This is the passage's cruellest word, and the commentators give it two faces. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ṣarīm* means to harvest, or to collect a crop from the fields, and that here it carries the sense of *masrūm* or *maqṭūʿ*: "harvested" or "cut." This signifies, it says, that the fire burnt the field and stripped it bare. They had sworn to reap the garden at dawn; by dawn it stood like a field already reaped — but not by them.

The word *ṣarīm* also means "night", and on that reading, as Mazhari notes, the verse signifies that the field became burnt up and black like night. Ibn Kathir preserves both strands from the early authorities: Ibn ʿAbbas said "like the dark night"; Ath-Thawri and As-Suddi both said "like the crop when it is harvested withered and dry."

## The march at dawn

Ayat 21–25 are almost cinematic. Everything the men do is brisk, competent and completely useless.

**"Then they called out to one another as morning broke" (21).** Ibn Kathir: when it was early morning they called each other so that they could go together to pick the harvest or cut it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: they were waking one another up early, urging that they should set out early if they wanted to harvest.

**"Go to your ḥarth in the morning, if you would pluck the fruits" (22).** Ibn Kathir renders **حَرْث** as "tilth" — cultivated land — and reads the conditional as "if you want to pluck your harvest fruit." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the description of the story given in these verses indicates that they did not only have a garden: they also had large tracts of land which they cultivated and fields of crops, possibly side by side with the orchard and in between the trees. They were called the owners of the garden, it explains, on account of the popularity of the garden.

**"So they set off, whispering to one another" (23).** Ibn Kathir: they spoke privately about what they were doing so that no one could hear what they were saying. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is exact about who they were hiding from: they were speaking in a low voice, lest a poor man should hear their talk and accompany them.

Then comes Ibn Kathir's observation, which is really the theological centre of these ayat: they whispered so that no one could hear — and then Allah, the All-Knower of secrets and private discussions, explained exactly what they were saying in private. Their whisper is now recited aloud across the earth. There is no such thing as a conversation Allah does not hear.

**"No poor person shall enter upon you into it today" (24).** Ibn Kathir: some of them said to others, "Do not allow any poor person to enter upon you in it today." And note the word **الْيَوْمَ**, "today". They were planning one morning; Allah was answering for the rest of their lives.

**"And they went in the morning with ḥard, qādirīn" (25).** This closing ayah of the passage is dense, and the commentators open it from different angles.

On **حَرْد**: Ibn Kathir takes it to mean "with strength and power." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the word means "to prevent" and "to express anger" — in other words, they thought they had the power to pick the fruit for themselves and prevent the poor from having a share in it, and that even if the poor did come to the garden, they had decided to chase them out. A footnote in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the word also means "to rush quickly", and that this is the sense adopted in Muhammad Taqi Usmani's translation of the text. Held together, the word paints men moving fast, hard-faced, with a settled intention to shut somebody out.

On **قَادِرِينَ**: Ibn Kathir's gloss is devastating in its restraint — "they thought they had power to do what they claimed and what they were desiring." The passage's final image, then, is of men striding out convinced that they are the ones with the power, at the precise moment when the only real Power has already ruled otherwise. The whole of ayah 25 is written from inside their heads. Ayah 20 already told us the truth.

## What to take from it

**Say inshaʼAllah, and mean it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it explicit: it is the Prophet's ﷺ way that when you mention you will do a particular work tomorrow, you attach it to the will of Allah. It is not a verbal tic. It is an admission that the night between you and your plan belongs to Him. These men were so confident in their plan that they never said the redeeming words, and they were undone in exactly that gap.

**Watch how easily generosity gets renamed as waste.** What the righteous father left on the ground — the fallen fruit, the grain after threshing — was food the poor of that place had come to depend on. His sons looked at the same practice and called their father foolish, and reasoned, in Ibn Kathir's report of their words, that "if we prevent them from it, then we will have more." That single re-description is the first move in this story, and everything else follows from it.

**Efficiency is not guidance.** Every practical decision these men made was sound: rise early, coordinate, keep it quiet, move fast. They failed on none of the things they were measuring, and lost everything on the one thing they were not.

**Nothing is off the record.** They spoke in a low voice so that a poor man would not overhear. Allah heard, and had it written down.

And underneath it all is Ibn Kathir's framing of the parable. This story was set before a people who had been given a great mercy and tremendous favours — above all the sending of Muhammad ﷺ among them — and who met that gift with denial, rejection and opposition. Makkah was being shown a mirror. Anyone who has been given something — wealth, health, knowledge, a Book — and has quietly begun calculating how to keep more of it from those who have come to depend on it is being shown the same mirror.

passages.title: Ruin, remorse, and the greater punishment
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are the second half of the parable of the People of the Garden: the moment the owners arrive at their orchard and find it destroyed, and everything that follows — confusion, realisation, rebuke, confession, mutual blame, and finally a hope turned back towards Allah. What holds them together is a single unbroken scene of discovery and remorse, sealed in ayah 33 by Allah's own verdict on it: this is how punishment comes, and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater still.

## The story behind the scene

Ibn Kathir explains that this whole passage is a parable Allah struck for the Quraysh, describing how they met His greatest favour — the sending of Muhammad ﷺ to them — with denial, rejection and opposition. The garden-owners stand for people who were given much and answered the gift with ingratitude.

In the ayat just before this passage, the owners had sworn an oath in the night that they would harvest the fruit at daybreak, deliberately early so that the poor and the beggars would not know, and so that no share of it would go out in charity. They swore it, Ibn Kathir notes, "without saying: If Allah wills" — and so Allah broke their oath. While they slept, a *tā'if* — a visitation — passed over the garden from their Lord: some heavenly destruction, as Ibn Kathir puts it. By morning it was *ka-s-sarīm*. Ibn Abbas said that means "like the dark night"; ath-Thawri and as-Suddi said "like the crop when it is harvested, withered and dry." They set off at dawn whispering to one another so no one would overhear the plan — and then, as Ibn Kathir says, Allah, the All-Knower of secrets and private discussions, explained what they were saying in private. They went out with *hard*, with strength and power, *qādirīn*: they thought they had power to do what they claimed and what they were desiring.

That is the moment ayah 26 opens on.

**Who were they?** Ibn Kathir reports that some of the Salaf said these people were from Yemen; Sa'id bin Jubayr said they were from a village called Darawan, six miles from San'a. It has also been said they were from the people of Ethiopia and were People of the Book, whose father had left them the garden. That father, the report says, handled it well: he ploughed back into the garden whatever it needed, kept aside a year's food for his dependants, and gave the excess away in charity. When he died and his children inherited, they said their father had been foolish to give the poor a share of the harvest — if they withheld it, they would have more. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the middle brother was righteous like his father, and that it used to please him to spend in the cause of Allah; he was not niggardly or stingy like the others.

## Ayat 26–27: two stages of realising

**"Indeed, we have gone astray."** When they arrived, Ibn Kathir says, the garden they had left in luster, brilliance and abundance of fruit was now black, gloomy and void of any benefit — so completely unrecognisable that their first thought was not that it had been destroyed, but that *they* had made a wrong turn. That is the force of *innā la-dāllūn*: as Ibn Abbas and others explained, "we have walked down a path other than the one we were seeking to reach it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly — not finding their garden on that spot, they first thought they must have lost their way and gone to the wrong place.

Then they looked at the surroundings, and the landmarks told them the truth. Ibn Kathir: "they changed their minds and realized with certainty that it was actually the correct path." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: they realised it was the right place they had come to, but the garden had been burnt up and destroyed.

**"No — we are the deprived ones."** Ibn Kathir renders the sense of ayah 27 as: "nay, this is it — but we have no portion and no share." Notice what has and has not shifted in the sequence the mufassirūn lay out. They now admit the loss, but the word they choose, *mahrūmūn*, "deprived", is still about their misfortune, not yet about their sin. It takes the middle brother's rebuke in the next ayah to move them further.

## Ayah 28: the one who had warned them

*Qāla awsatuhum* — "the awsat among them said." Ibn Kathir records a striking consensus on this word: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ikrimah, Muhammad bin Ka'b, ar-Rabi' bin Anas, ad-Dahhak and Qatadah all said it means the most just of them and the best of them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies him as the middle brother, the best of them, righteous like his father.

His rebuke is a question: *a-lam aqul lakum lawlā tusabbihūn* — "did I not tell you: why do you not perform tasbīh?" *Tasbīh*, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, literally means to pronounce Allah's purity. The early scholars read his words in two ways, and Ibn Kathir preserves both:

- Mujahid, as-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj all said it means "why do you not say, *in shā' Allāh* — if Allah wills." As-Suddi explained that making an exception for the will of Allah was, in that time, done by glorifying Allah (tasbīh). Ibn Jarir said simply: "it is a person's saying, 'If Allah wills.'" On this reading the brother is pointing straight back at the oath they had sworn with no exception made for Allah's will.
- It has also been said that he meant: why do you not glorify Allah and thank Him for what He has given you and favoured you with?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, draws out what their silence about Allah actually implied. They were withholding the poor's share out of fear that their fruit would be depleted and would not be replenished by Allah if they gave the poor their due. The brother was telling them that Allah is pure of such pettiness — and that those who spend in the way of Allah do not merely have their wealth made full again or what they spent replaced, but are given over and above what they spent.

## Ayah 29: confession, one morning too late

*Subhāna rabbinā innā kunnā zālimīn* — "Glory to our Lord! Truly we were wrongdoers." They finally say the words he had asked them for. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that neither of the brothers had paid heed to his advice at the time; only when the damage was done did they admit that Allah is Pure, free from any qualities of weakness and shortcoming, and that they were the wrongdoers — unjust to the poor, intending to deprive them of their share and devour it themselves.

Ibn Kathir's comment here is one of the most sobering lines in the passage: "They became obedient when it was of no benefit to them, and they were remorseful and confessed when it was not of any use."

**A warning from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** Although the best of the three brothers offered the right advice, he joined the other brothers in following their wrong opinion — and so he suffered the same loss. The lesson drawn there is direct: anyone who prevents other people from committing sins but does not abstain from them himself and joins them in the wrong acts will suffer the same fate as the others. Speaking the truth does not exempt a person from acting on it.

## Ayah 30: turning on each other

*Fa-aqbala ba'duhum 'alā ba'din yatalāwamūn* — "then they turned to one another, trading blame." Ibn Kathir: they started blaming each other for what they had resolved to do, preventing the poor from receiving their right of the harvested fruit — so that their response to each other was only to confess their error and sin.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the observation: at the beginning they made an admission of guilt, but then they turned to face each other in mutual accusation, blaming each other for the punishment that visited them — yet the crime was not committed by only a single person among them; it was committed jointly by all or most of them. And it adds a note of caution for our own times: a common misdeed in our days is that when a calamity befalls a group of people because of their collective conduct, an additional scourge befalls them — instead of reforming themselves, they start wasting their time accusing each other.

## Ayah 31: from blame to repentance

*Yā waylanā innā kunnā tāghīn* — "Woe to us! We were indeed transgressors." Ibn Kathir unpacks *tāghīn* as: "we have transgressed, trespassed, violated and exceeded the bounds until this happened to us."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the movement of the scene: at first they accused one another of the sin; then, when they considered the matter carefully, they admitted that they were all in the wrong. They lamented and admitted their guilt, and that amounted to repentance — and it was on the basis of that repentance that they hoped Allah would give them in exchange a garden better than the one destroyed.

## Ayah 32: hope turned back to Allah

*'Asā rabbunā an yubdilanā khayran minhā, innā ilā rabbinā rāghibūn* — "We hope that our Lord will give us in exchange better than it. Truly, we hope in our Lord."

Ibn Kathir records two views on what they were hoping for, without deciding between them: it has been said they were hoping for something better in exchange in this life, and it has also been said they were hoping for its reward in the abode of the Hereafter — "and Allah knows best."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays a report supporting the first view: Imam Baghawi reports from Sayyidnā Abdullah Ibn Mas'ud that, according to his information, when these brothers repented truly, Allah blessed them with a better vineyard that bore such large bunches of grapes that a single bunch could be loaded on a mule.

Read ayat 26 to 32 as one line and they are the anatomy of a heart coming back: bewilderment, then admission of loss, then rebuke, then declaring Allah's purity, then blaming one another, then owning the wrong together, then turning to Allah in hope. Their loss was real; their end was not despair.

## Ayah 33: the verdict

*Kadhālika l-'adhāb* — "such is the punishment." Ibn Kathir reads this as a general principle: such is the punishment of whoever opposes the command of Allah, is stingy with what Allah has given him and favoured him with, withholds the right of the poor and needy, and responds to Allah's blessings upon him with ungratefulness.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the ayah in the surah's flow: after a brief reference to the famine faced by the Makkans and a detailed account of the People of the Garden whose garden was burnt as a punishment, this ayah sets down a general rule — when a Divine punishment visits, it visits in this way. And it makes a point worth pausing on: this kind of punishment in the mortal world does not serve as an expiation for the punishment in the Hereafter. Losing the garden did not settle the account.

Hence the closing weight: *wa-la-'adhābu l-ākhirati akbar, law kānū ya'lamūn* — "and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they but knew." Ibn Kathir: this is the punishment in this life, as you have heard, and the punishment of the Hereafter is even harder. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the same: the punishment of the Hereafter is greater and more severe.

## Living it

The passage is unusually concrete about what it asks:

**Say "in shā' Allāh" and mean it.** On the reading of Mujahid, as-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarir, the brother's rebuke points straight back at an oath sworn with no exception made for Allah's will — and Ibn Kathir says it was for that reason that Allah broke their vow. Attaching your plans to Allah's will is not a verbal habit; it is an admission of who actually controls outcomes.

**Do not treat the poor's share as your loss.** Mazhari's point in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the fear directly: withholding out of anxiety that giving will deplete you imputes to Allah a pettiness He is pure of. Those who spend in His way have their wealth made full again, and are given over and above what they spent.

**Beware of inheriting wealth and discarding the habits attached to it.** The father gave the excess away every year; the sons called that foolishness — and Ibn Kathir's report ends with Allah taking away all they possessed of wealth, gain and charity, so that nothing remained for them.

**Advice you give must bind you too.** The best of the brothers still went along with them — and still suffered the same loss.

**When trouble strikes a family or a community, do not spend it on blame.** Ibn Kathir shows the blaming producing nothing but a confession of error and sin; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the mutual accusation an additional scourge on top of the calamity. The turn that helped them came in ayat 31 and 32, when they admitted that they were all in the wrong, and then turned to their Lord.

**And keep the ceiling in view.** Even total worldly loss is the smaller punishment, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that it does not expiate what comes after. Ayah 33 refuses to let the reader treat a ruined garden as the end of the reckoning.

passages.title: By what do you judge? The Day they cannot prostrate
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Having just told at length the story of the People of the Garden — men whose garden was burnt as a punishment when they disobeyed Allah and opposed His commands — Allah now turns on the objection that lies underneath all denial of the Hereafter: the suspicion that in the end it makes no real difference how a person lives. Ayat 34–43 answer that suspicion twice. First by argument: the claim that the obedient and the criminal will end up the same is put on trial and asked for its evidence (35–41). Then by scene: the Day arrives, and the difference between the two is made visible in a single gesture — who can still bow, and who cannot (42–43).

## Where we have just come from

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that ayah 33 — *"In this way the punishment comes. And, of course, the punishment of the Hereafter is even greater, if they but realize!"* — is the hinge. After a brief reference to the famine faced by the Makkans and a detailed account of the People of the Garden whose garden was burnt as a punishment, this ayah sets down a general rule: when a divine punishment visits, it visits in this way, and a punishment of this kind in the mortal world does not serve as an expiation for the punishment of the Hereafter. What waits there is greater and more severe.

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 34 as the deliberate counterpart to that story. After mentioning the situation of the people of the worldly garden and the wrath they suffered when they disobeyed Allah and opposed His commands, Allah explains that whoever has taqwā of Him will have **"Gardens of Delight with their Lord."** And Ibn Kathir presses the one thing the burnt garden could never offer: *permanence*. These Gardens in the Hereafter "will never end… will last forever and their pleasures will never cease."

Their garden was burnt away in this world. This one does not end.

The word *taqwā* is left untranslated by Ibn Kathir — "those who have Taqwa" — and the translation before us renders the same group simply as **"the righteous."** They are the exact opposite of the men in the story just told. And the reward is described as being **"with their Lord."**

## The claim that is put on trial

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies precisely what ayat 35 onward are refuting. The pagans of Makkah denied that the Resurrection would ever occur; they thought the story of Resurrection and accountability was fiction. And they added a second thought on top of the first: even if that did happen, they thought, they would get the same type of blessings and wealth there as they have in this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict on that assumption is blunt: it is "a strange sort of assertion for which they have no authority, nor proof nor any celestial book. Nor is there any promise from Allah that they will get the same type of blessings."

Against it comes ayah 35, which Ibn Kathir renders: **"Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?"** He unpacks the question as: *should We deal equally between them in terms of recompense?* — and answers it with force: *"Nay, by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, surely not!"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same rhetorical question in other words: *shall We make the obedient like the sinners?*

Notice what the two words name: on one side those who have submitted, on the other the criminals — the obedient and the sinners. To ask whether the two receive the same recompense is to ask whether the difference between them was ever real.

Then ayah 36: **"What is the matter with you? How do you judge?"** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and cutting — *how can you think that?* The verb is *taḥkumūn*, "you judge, you pass a verdict". They are not offering an opinion; they are handing down rulings about how the universe will settle its accounts. Hold on to that verb, because it returns in ayah 39, and it is the thread running through the whole cross-examination.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: why the Day of Judgement is rationally necessary

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the passage its longest and most useful treatment. These ayat, it says, "give a solid proof to the necessity of the Day of Judgment, because accountability, rewarding the righteous and punishing the evil are all rationally necessary." The argument runs like this.

It is witnessed by every person in this mortal world, and no one can deny, that the wicked, the evil, the unjust, the thieves and the bandits generally lead a comfortable and enjoyable life here. A thief or a bandit sometimes gains in one night so much wealth that a righteous person might not gain as much in his entire life. The former has no fear of Allah or of the Hereafter, nor any sense of shame; he fulfils his selfish desires as he likes, by hook or by crook. The latter fears Allah — and if he does not have that, his sense of shame among his brotherhood overwhelms him. In short, in this world the wicked and the evil ones seem to be successful, and the good people seem to be unsuccessful.

If there never arises an occasion where fair play and justice is established — where the good are rewarded and the evil are punished — then, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues, several things collapse at once. It would be meaningless to refer to evil as evil. There would be no reason to stop a person from fulfilling his selfish desires and doing evil acts. Justice itself would have no meaning or significance. And the believer in Allah's existence is left facing a question: *where is Allah's justice?*

Then the obvious objection is raised and answered. Someone may argue that a criminal *is* apprehended, exposed to disgrace and punished; that the laws and statutes of a government already establish standards of justice and fair play, separating the innocent from the evil right here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān replies that this is incorrect. It is not possible for a government to keep an eye on everyone, everywhere, in all circumstances. Where a crime does happen to be seen, gathering the judicial evidence needed to convict is no easy task. And even where the evidence could be gathered, there are several escape doors through which the guilty may get away: force, bribery, intercession and pressure. Review the punishment history of present-day governments and courts, it says, and it appears that nowadays only those people are punished who are foolish, brainless and helpless or without support — not cunning enough to find a loophole or an escape route, without money to pay for bribery, without an influential person to back them or intercede for them. The rest of the criminals are moving freely.

That is the shape of the argument. Commenting on ayah 35, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: it is rationally necessary that there should come a time when people will have to give account of their deeds — a place where the guilty will find no escape routes, an ideal world of absolute justice and fair play where good and evil are clearly distinguished. If this is not the state of affairs in the Hereafter, then no evil should be evil and no sin should be sin in this mortal world, and divine justice would be rendered meaningless.

## The cross-examination: ayat 37–41

Having exposed the claim, Allah demands its credentials. The ayat come as a chain of "Or have you…?" questions — each one a door being tried and found locked. This is the form of a formal challenge: name your source of knowledge.

**A scripture? (37–38)** *"Or have you a Book wherein you learn, that you shall therein have all that you choose?"* Ibn Kathir spells out the force of *tadrusūn*, "you learn": *is there in your hands a Book that has been sent down from heaven that you study, memorize and pass on to each other, the latter generations conveying it from the generations of old? Do you have such a Book, containing definite laws, as you claim?*

And what would this imagined book say? Ayah 38: **"all that you choose."** That is the tell. The "revelation" they are relying on is one that would hand them whatever they chose. They have not consulted a book; they have consulted their own preferences.

**A sworn covenant? (39)** *"Or have you oaths from Us, lasting until the Day of Judgement, that yours will be what you judge?"* Ibn Kathir: *do you have covenants and confirmed agreements with Us?* The wording is striking — oaths binding **upon Us**, running all the way to the Day of Resurrection. If Allah were going to be obliged to deliver what they assume, only a promise from Him could oblige Him, and it would have to be a promise with no expiry. And what would the promise cover? Ibn Kathir explains **"that yours will be what you judge"** as: *that you will attain all that you want and desire.* There is *taḥkumūn* again, the same verb as in ayah 36. Their theory of the next life is not a judgement about reality; it is a wish given a verdict's grammar.

**A guarantor? (40)** *"Ask them, which of them will stand as surety for that!"* Ibn Kathir renders the meaning as: say to them, *"Who is the sponsor of guarantee this?"* — and reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said it means, *"Which of them will be guarantor for that?"* This is the language of contracts. When a claim has no document behind it, you ask for a person who will put his own name against it. Let one of them step forward and personally underwrite the claim that the criminal and the one who submits end in the same place.

**Backers? (41)** *"Or have they 'partners'? Then let them bring their 'partners' if they are truthful!"* Ibn Kathir: *do they have idols and rival gods besides Allah?* The challenge is deliberately physical — bring them here. The last door is tried, and it is locked like the others.

So the passage walks their claim past every possible source of authority — a revealed text, a sworn covenant, a personal guarantee, a divine backer — and finds it standing on nothing at all.

## Ayah 42: the Day the Shin is laid bare

Then the argument stops and the curtain lifts. Ibn Kathir explains that after mentioning that those who have taqwā will have Gardens of Delight with their Lord, Allah explains *when* this will be and its actual occurrence: **"The Day when the Shin shall be laid bare and they shall be called to prostrate themselves, but they shall not be able to do so."** He glosses the Day itself as "the Day of Judgement and the horrors, earthquakes, trials, tests and great matters that will occur during it."

Here Ibn Kathir cites a hadith. Al-Bukhari recorded that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said that he heard the Prophet ﷺ saying: *"Our Lord will reveal His Shin, and every believing male and female will prostrate to Him. The only people who will remain standing are those who prostrated in the worldly life only to be seen and heard (showing off). This type of person will try to prostrate at that time, but his back will made to be one stiff plate (the bone will not bend or flex)."* Ibn Kathir adds that this hadith was recorded in the Two Sahihs and other books from different routes of transmission with various wordings, and that it is a long hadith that is very popular.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise notes that these ayat go on to describe the horrors of the Day of Judgment and the punishment of the evil ones, "including the description of the exposure of the Shin [ kashf-us-saq ] in Verse 42" — and refers the reader, for the explanation of that phrase, to a footnote on the translation of that verse. That footnote is not part of the material before us, so nothing further about it is offered here; what the two commentaries do give us is the wording of the ayah, the hadith as al-Bukhari recorded it, and Ibn Kathir's sense of the Day it names: terror, upheaval, and matters of overwhelming gravity.

## Ayah 43: the punishment shaped like the crime

**"Their eyes will be cast down and ignominy will cover them; they used to be called to prostrate themselves, while they were…"**

Ibn Kathir draws out the exactness of it. Their cast-down eyes and the ignominy that covers them are "in the final abode, due to their crimes and arrogance in the worldly life. Thus they will be punished with the opposite of what they did." When they were called to prostrate in the worldly life, he says, they refused to do so **even though they were healthy and secure** — no illness in the body, no fear for their lives, nothing preventing them but themselves. Therefore they will be punished with the lack of ability to do so in the Hereafter.

The scene is then described plainly. When the Almighty Lord makes Himself visible before the believers, the believers will fall down in prostration to Him, but no one of the disbelievers and the hypocrites will be able to prostrate; rather, their backs will become one plate. Every time one of them attempts to prostrate, he will bow his neck but will not be able to go down. And Ibn Kathir names the symmetry directly: "This is just like in the life of this world, when these people were in opposition to what the believers were doing." The body on that Day simply displays the posture the soul had already chosen.

Note who else stands among them in that hadith: the one who *did* prostrate in this life, but only to be seen and heard. He performed the outward act and it did not hold.

## Living it

**Take the argument seriously when the world looks unjust.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is not asking you to pretend the wicked struggle. It concedes plainly that they prosper, that no government can watch everyone, and that force, bribery, intercession and pressure open escape doors for those who can afford them. The believer's answer is not to deny what he sees, but to know that a time is coming when the account is given in a place where the guilty find no escape routes.

**Test your own claim about the Hereafter.** The disbelievers' error was not that they had weak evidence; it was that they had none — no authority, no proof, no celestial book, no promise from Allah — and never noticed, because the conclusion was the one they preferred (ayah 38). It is worth asking of any confident assumption about how Allah will deal with us: is this something Allah has told us, or something I would choose?

**Guard the sujūd.** Ayah 43 makes prostration the measure, and the reason Ibn Kathir gives is that they were *healthy and secure* when the call came. Health and safety are the very conditions in which the call is answered or refused — which means the ordinary, unremarkable prayer performed today, in a body that still bends, is precisely what is being weighed. And the hadith adds the second warning: let it be for Allah, not to be seen and heard, so that when the great call comes, the back that has bowed all its life bows once more.

passages.title: Leave them to Me: respite is not reprieve
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a question that was being pressed hard on the Prophet ﷺ: if these people are truly guilty, and Allah truly has the power to punish, why is nothing happening to them? The answer comes in two movements — first Allah takes the case out of the Prophet's ﷺ hands entirely (ayat 44–45), then He turns to the deniers and shows they have no ground to stand on at all (ayat 46–47).

Immediately before these ayat, the surah has been describing the Day when the Shin shall be laid bare and people are called to prostrate — which Ibn Kathir explains as the Day of Judgement, with the horrors, earthquakes, trials and great matters that will occur during it. Their arrogance now, their humiliation then. Ayah 44 picks up from exactly that point — *and in the meantime, what about them?*

## "So leave Me alone with him" (ayah 44)

**فَذَرْنِي وَمَن يُكَذِّبُ بِهَٰذَا الْحَدِيثِ** — "So, leave Me alone with those who reject this discourse," in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering; "Then leave Me alone with such as belie this narration," in Ibn Kathir's.

Ibn Kathir reads it as it sounds — as **a severe threat**. He gives the sense as: *leave Me alone with this person; I know about him and how I will gradually punish him and increase him in his falsehood. I am giving him respite for a while, then I will seize him with a mighty and powerful punishment.*

The restraint of the phrasing is part of what makes it weighty. Allah does not say "I will destroy him." He says: *leave him to Me.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second layer that sits alongside the first: in the original Arabic, "so leave me alone" is an idiomatic expression, and what it signifies is **"Rely on Allah."** The command, on this reading, carries an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ himself — not a call to action but a call to trust.

Both readings stand together, and they explain why this ayah lands exactly where it does.

**"This hadith"** — *bi hādhā al-hadīth*. The word is rendered variously as "this message", "this discourse", "this narration"; Ibn Kathir states plainly what is meant: **the Qur'an**. It is worth pausing on that. The Qur'an is named here not by a title of majesty but by a plain word for speech, for an account, for something narrated. To reject it is not to lose an argument. It is to be left to Allah.

## The occasion: a demand for punishment, and a Prophet's heart

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives us the human situation behind the words. The disbelievers **often demanded Divine punishment**, arguing that if they are really guilty in the sight of Allah, and if He has the power to punish, then why does the punishment not befall them forthwith?

Maʿārif calls these **"heart-rending demands"** — and says that on account of them, the thought probably must have crossed the mind of the Prophet ﷺ, and he might have prayed to Allah to punish them at some point, **in the hope that the rest of the people might draw lessons and amend their conduct.** Even the thought of punishment, in his ﷺ heart, was tied to the hope of others being guided.

It was on that occasion, Maʿārif says, that Allah revealed ayah 45: that He is **the best aware of the wisdom behind His decisions.** He does not punish them immediately; He gives them respite **to test them and to give them an opportunity to believe.**

Notice what that does to the whole passage. The delay that the deniers read as proof that there is nothing to fear is in fact an open door — held open by the One they are mocking.

## The blessing that is not a blessing (ayah 44)

**سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُم مِّنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ** — "We shall punish them gradually from directions they perceive not," in Ibn Kathir's rendering; "We will draw them on little by little (towards Hell) from a way they do not know," in Maʿārif's.

Both renderings carry the same shape: *gradually*, *little by little*. Not a sudden fall but a descent taken in stages. And the deadliest part is where it comes from — *min haythu lā yaʿlamūn*, from a way they do not know. Not from a quarter they are watching. Not through anything that looks like punishment.

Ibn Kathir spells out how it works: **they will not even be aware of it. Rather, they will believe that it is a noble blessing from Allah, but really the same matter is actually a form of humiliation for them.** The gift is the trap. Profit, growing family, untroubled years — received by a heart that denies, these become rungs of a ladder going down.

He supports this with two other places in the Qur'an:

- *"Do they think that in wealth and children with which We expand them, We hasten unto them with good things? Nay, but they perceive not."* (23:55–56)
- *"So, when they forgot that which they had been reminded, We opened for them the gates of everything, until in the midst of their enjoyment in that which they were given, all of a sudden, We punished them, and lo! They were plunged into destruction with deep regrets and sorrows."* (6:44)

Read those two together and the pattern is unmistakable: **forgetting the reminder, then every door opening.** It is why a believer never reads worldly ease — his own or anyone else's — as a verdict of divine approval.

## Respite, and the grip that does not slip (ayah 45)

**وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ** — "And I will grant them a respite." Ibn Kathir gives the sense as: *I will delay them, give them respite and extend their time.* It is not a pardon; it is a **term being allowed to run on**.

Then the sentence turns: **إِنَّ كَيْدِي مَتِينٌ** — "Verily, My plan is strong."
