Ibn Kathir continues the sense: *Yet, this is My plan, and My plot against them* — and "strong" here means **great against whoever opposes My command, rejects My Messengers and dares to disobey Me.** Note carefully where it is aimed: not at the innocent, but at those who have set themselves against His command and His Messengers. Their move is answered, and what answers it does not fail.

Ibn Kathir then brings the hadith that is practically the commentary on this ayah. **In the Two Sahihs** it is recorded from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said:

> "Verily Allah the Exalted gives respite to the wrongdoer until He seizes him and he will not be able to escape Him."

And he ﷺ then recited:

> *"Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Verily, His punishment is painful and severe."* (11:102)

That is the passage's thesis in one line: **respite is not reprieve.** The rope is being paid out, not cut. And when the hand closes, nothing slips through it.

## Two questions that close every exit (ayat 46–47)

Having settled the matter of the deniers with Allah, the passage turns to the deniers themselves with two questions.

**Ayah 46: "Or is it that you ask them for a wage, so that they are heavily burdened with debt?"** Is there a *fee*? Is the Messenger ﷺ charging them something so crushing — *maghram*, a debt, a financial burden — that walking away is simply the sensible choice? Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *you, O Muhammad, call them to Allah without taking any wages from them; rather, you hope for the reward with Allah.* There is no invoice. That excuse is gone.

**Ayah 47: "Or that the Unseen is in their hands, so that they can write it down?"** Then perhaps they hold knowledge the Messenger ﷺ does not — is the Unseen in their possession, so that they are the ones doing the recording? The question is put, and the answer is plain. Ibn Kathir notes that the explanation of these two ayat has already been given in Sūrat aṭ-Ṭūr, where the same pair appears.

So what is left? Ibn Kathir states the conclusion bluntly: **they reject that which he brought to them simply due to ignorance, disbelief and obstinacy.** Not evidence. Not cost. Not knowledge. Just refusal.

This is why ayat 46–47 belong with 44–45 rather than standing apart. Ayah 44 says *their case is Mine*; ayat 46–47 show that when the case is opened, there is nothing in their defence at all.

## The comfort of Yūnus (peace be upon him)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that towards the end of the surah the story of Sayyidnā Yūnus (peace be upon him) is concisely told — and that it comes as comfort to the Prophet ﷺ on exactly this issue.

When his people constantly demanded punishment, he became indignant and prayed for the punishment to be sent down. The signs of the punishment started appearing. He left the place and transferred himself elsewhere. In the meantime the entire nation wept, wailed, sincerely repented and begged refuge from the Divine punishment — and Allah pardoned them and took the punishment away. Yūnus (peace be upon him) felt embarrassed, thinking that if he went back to his people they might think he was a liar. As a result, without the clear permission of Allah, he acted purely on his *ijtihād* (independent judgement) that he would not go back to them. At this, Allah, in order to caution him, created a situation where he had to undertake a sea voyage, and was then lowered into the sea where he was swallowed up by a fish. Being thus cautioned, he sought the Divine pardon — and Allah once again opened the doors of the former blessings to be restored to him. Maʿārif notes that the full description of the event is given in Sūrah Yūnus (10:98) and other surahs.

The lesson Maʿārif draws is precise, and it is the lesson of our passage: **the Prophet ﷺ is comforted by this story not to be impressed by people's demands, nor to be anxious to get them punished hastily. Allah's wisdom is profound and unfathomable. Allah alone knows what is in the best interests of the world. Allah should be trusted and relied on.**

The punishment that the people of Yūnus begged to have lifted *was* lifted — because they repented. Had it fallen on the day it was demanded, an entire nation would have been lost.

## Living it

**Do not read prosperity as approval.** Not other people's, and not your own. Ibn Kathir's warning cuts both ways: the thing that feels like "a noble blessing from Allah" may be the opposite. The test of a blessing is what it does to your obedience.

**Do not read delay as absence.** The taunt behind ayah 44 is still made, in newer language: *nothing has happened to them, therefore nothing will.* The hadith in the Two Sahihs answers it — respite is given to the wrongdoer, and then the seizing comes, and there is no escaping it.

**Leave it to Allah.** *Fadharnī* — leave them to Me. And Maʿārif's reading of the idiom is the practical one for anyone carrying anger at an injustice he cannot fix: **rely on Allah.** Give the reminder; leave the reckoning where it belongs.

**Do not be in a hurry for the door to close.** The Prophet ﷺ may have wished for punishment hoping others would take heed — and the answer came that Allah gives respite to test them and to give them an opportunity to believe, followed by the story of a nation that used its last hours to weep and was forgiven. Delay is opportunity. That includes the delay you have been given.

passages.title: Be patient, and not like the man of the fish
passages.tafsir:
These are the closing ayat of Sūrat al-Qalam, addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah tells him to hold his ground under the pressure of his people's rejection (48), warns him against the haste of one earlier prophet (48–50), then shows what that pressure looked like — hate-filled stares and the taunt "he is a madman" (51) — before sealing the sūrah with the verdict on the Book they mocked: it is a Reminder for all the worlds (52).

What holds the passage together is a single instruction unfolded in two directions. Inward: *be patient* — and here is what haste once cost a prophet. Outward: *here is what you are being patient with* — their eyes and their tongues — and here is why it is worth it.

## "So be patient with your Lord's decree" (48)

Ibn Kathir reads the opening command as spoken to the Prophet ﷺ in the thick of his people's rejection: persevere against the harm your people cause you and their rejection, *for Allah will give you authority over them, and make the final victory for you and your followers in this life and the Hereafter.* So this ṣabr — patient endurance — is not resignation. It is waiting on a decree already guaranteed to land in your favour: the patience of someone who knows the outcome and is only being asked to endure the interval.

The word is *ḥukm*: your Lord's judgement, His decision. Ibn Kathir underlines why patience with it is the only sane response — **Allah is the One whose execution of divine decree cannot be resisted.** Nothing hurries it, and nothing obstructs it.

## "And do not be like the man of the fish" (48)

Then the warning, and it is startling — the Prophet ﷺ is told not to be like *a prophet*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the title plainly: he is called **ṣāḥib al-ḥūt, "the man of the fish," because he was devoured by a fish and remained in its belly for some time.** Ibn Kathir names him — Dhun-Nūn, Yūnus ibn Mattā — and identifies precisely what is being warned against. Not disbelief, not disobedience of the kind we usually imagine, but that **he went off angry with his people.** Ibn Kathir titles the whole passage accordingly: *the command to be patient and to refrain from being hasty as Yūnus was.* The fault named here is haste.

Ibn Kathir then walks through what followed, and it is worth feeling rather than skimming: riding on a ship at sea; being swallowed by a great fish; the fish carrying him off into the ocean; being in the darkness and depth of the sea, hearing the sea and its dwellers glorifying the Most High, the Most Able. A man in total blackness, surrounded by a whole creation doing exactly what he had walked away from — staying in place and glorifying Allah.

**"When he cried out" — *idh nādā*.** Ayah 48 catches him at the moment of the call. The Qur'an adds that he was *makẓūm*; Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and as-Suddī all explained it as "while he was distressed."** Not composed, not eloquent — choked with grief. And what came out of that choked throat, as Ibn Kathir quotes, was a call from the layers of darkness:

> *"There is no god but You, glorified are You! Truly I have been of the wrongdoers."* (21:87)

Notice its shape. No request at all. He declares Allah's oneness, declares Allah free of any fault in what has befallen him, and takes the blame entirely onto himself. Allah's response is quoted straight after: *"So We answered his call and delivered him from the distress. And thus do We deliver the believers"* (21:88) — the last clause turning a one-off rescue into a standing promise.

## "Had he not been shown grace by his Lord…" (49)

Ayah 49 is a *what would have happened*, and the commentators unpack it carefully.

Ibn Kathir sets it beside another ayah: *"Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained inside its belly till the Day they are resurrected"* (37:143–144). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the reading of **Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanawi**, who takes "a favour from his Lord" to mean **the acceptance of his repentance**, and "the wilderness" (Ibn Kathir's rendering: "the naked shore") to mean **the place where he was thrown by the fish**. Read together with 37:143–144, three possibilities line up:

- Had he not offered *tasbīḥ* (glorification of Allah) and *tawbah* (repentance) at all, he would have remained in the fish's belly for good;
- Had he repented but not been favoured with the *acceptance* of that repentance, the fish would still have cast him out into the wilderness — but **in a reproachable state**, still under blame;
- Since Allah did favour him with the acceptance of his repentance, he was no longer reproachable at all.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records that **some other scholars** understand "the wilderness" here as **the plain of the Gathering (Ḥashr)**: had his repentance not been accepted, he would have been cast into that plain in a reproachable state. The sources give both readings without ruling between them, and so should we.

Either way ayah 49 stands: what saved him was not his own endurance, nor even the bare act of repenting, but *a favour from his Lord that reached him* — grace arriving in time.

## "Then his Lord chose him" (50)

Ayah 50 is the resolution, and it is astonishingly generous. *Fajtabāhu rabbuh* — **his Lord chose him**, singled him out — *and made him one of the righteous.* The man who went off angry and was swallowed by the sea is not merely forgiven; he is chosen.

Ibn Kathir attaches to this a warning against ever holding the slip against him. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"It is not befitting for anyone to say that I am better than Yūnus ibn Mattā."**

Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī recorded this ḥadīth as well, and that it is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs on the authority of Abū Hurayrah.

Sit with the pairing. In ayah 48 the Prophet ﷺ is told *do not be like him* — and by the Prophet's ﷺ own tongue we are forbidden to claim to be better than him. Here the Qur'an mentions a prophet's lapse to teach, not to demean. The lesson is aimed at *us*: take the warning about haste, and take with it a firm prohibition on looking down at the one it was drawn from.

## "They would almost trip you with their eyes" (51)

Now the passage turns to what the Prophet ﷺ was being asked to be patient *with*.

**The verb.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing **Rāghib**, derives *la-yuzliqūnaka* from *izlāq*, meaning **"to trip up, to cause someone to fall, or to make a mistake."** Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others** glossed it: *in order to have some effect on you.*

Two complementary explanations are given of *with their eyes*:

**1. The look of hatred.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the disbelievers cast such angry looks at him that they might frighten him into giving up his mission or intimidate him into yielding to their pressure tactics — glaring with such hatred and anger as if they were to make him slip from his standpoint. Anyone who has been stared down for their faith knows this exactly.

**2. The evil eye.** Ibn Kathir: *"they will affect you by looking at you with their eyes"* — meaning **they are jealous of you due to their hatred of you, and were it not for Allah's protection of you and His defending you against them, their evil eye would harm you.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a background for the second reading, reported by **Imam Baghawi and some other commentators**: there was a person famous in Arabia for casting the evil eye on camels or animals, causing instant death or destruction. **The pagans of Arabia** were enemies of the Prophet ﷺ and left no stone unturned in harming him; they even contemplated afflicting him with an evil eye, and so decided to secure the services of that particular man, instructing him to cast the eye on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that he would become ill. **He exerted himself to the utmost, but to no avail** — Allah protected him and he was unaffected. These ayat were revealed in connection with that incident.

That is the sting in ayah 51's wording: they would *almost* trip you. Almost — and not.

## The evil eye is real

Ibn Kathir states that this ayah is a proof that **the effect of the evil eye and its affliction, by the command of Allah, is real**, and that many ḥadīths on it have been reported through numerous routes of transmission. Among those he cites:

- **Muslim** recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The evil eye is real. If anything were to overtake the divine decree, it would be the evil eye. And if you perform ghusl, then wash well."* (Ibn Kathir notes Muslim was alone in recording this; al-Bukhārī did not mention it.)
- **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Verily, the evil eye is real."* Ibn Kathir notes that **both al-Bukhārī and Muslim** recorded it as well. Ibn Mājah also recorded from Abū Hurayrah, *"The evil eye is real"* — Ibn Kathir notes Ibn Mājah was alone in that wording.
- **Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays** said, "O Messenger of Allah, Banū Jaʿfar are afflicted with the evil eye; should I seek ruqyah?" He ﷺ replied: *"Yes — for if anything could overcome the divine decree, it would be the evil eye."* Recorded by Imam Ahmad, and likewise by at-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and an-Nasāʾī; **at-Tirmidhī said: "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."**

Note the theological care in that wording, in both narrations: *if anything could* overtake the decree — a hypothetical the Prophet ﷺ never affirms. Nothing overtakes the decree of Allah. As Ibn Kathir puts it, the evil eye has its effect *by the command of Allah*; it is a real cause, and it does not out-run Him.

**What the Sunnah prescribes against it**, all from the same sources:

- **Ruqyah** — praying over the afflicted for healing. Ibn Mājah recorded from Buraydah ibn al-Ḥuṣayb that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"There is no ruqyah except to cure the evil eye and the sting"* — though Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Buraydah himself without attributing it to the Prophet ﷺ, and that al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī recorded it from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, likewise unattributed to him ﷺ. Ibn Mājah also recorded from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **ordered her to have ruqyah performed as a cure against the evil eye**; Ibn Kathir notes this was reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
- **The two protective sūrahs.** Ibn Mājah recorded that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to seek refuge from the evil eye of the jinn and the evil eye of humans — **then, when the Muʿawwidhatān were revealed, he used them and abandoned everything else.** Also recorded by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī; at-Tirmidhī said "Ḥasan."
- **Protecting children.** It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to invoke Allah's protection for al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn with: *"I seek protection for you two by the perfect Words of Allah from every devil and dangerous creature, and from every eye that is evil,"* adding, *"Thus did Ibrāhīm seek protection for Isḥāq and Ismāʿīl."* Recorded by al-Bukhārī and the Sunan compilers.
- **Jibrīl's ruqyah for the Prophet ﷺ.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Saʿīd that Jibrīl came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked whether he was suffering from any ailment; he said yes, and Jibrīl said: *"In the Name of Allah I pray over you for healing, from everything that bothers you, from the evil of every soul and every evil eye that hates you; may Allah cure you. In the Name of Allah I pray over you for healing."* Recorded by Muslim and the Sunan compilers except Abū Dāwūd.

**And the duty on the one who looks.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out on a journey and the Companions came with him to the valley of Kharrār near al-Juḥfah. They stopped there and Sahl bathed. ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah looked at him and exclaimed that he had never seen skin so fine — and Sahl at once had a seizure and fell to the ground, not lifting his head or regaining consciousness. Brought to the Prophet ﷺ, he asked, "Do you hold anyone responsible for what has happened to him?" They said ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah had looked at him. The Prophet ﷺ called him and **was very angry with him**, saying:

> *"Would one of you knowingly kill his brother? Why do you not ask Allah to bless your brother when you see something of him that you like?"*

He then told ʿĀmir, *"Bathe for him"* — and ʿĀmir washed his face, hands, elbows, knees, feet and the inside of his waist-wrapper into a drinking vessel, and that water was poured over Sahl, who recovered and left with the people with nothing wrong with him. In another narration, recorded by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, Ibn Kathir preserves the general rule from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: *"If one of you sees in his brother, or in himself, or in his wealth, something that pleases him, then let him ask Allah to bless it — for verily, the evil eye is real."*

This is the practical heart of it. The evil eye is not chiefly something to fear from others; it is something to guard others from. Admiration left as bare admiration can wound. When you see something you like, turn it into a prayer — ask Allah to bless it. The Arabic of the ḥadīth is *fal-yubarrik*, from *barakah*: Allah's blessing, the divine goodness that makes a thing endure and increase. Ask for that, and your delight becomes a gift to the one you are looking at instead of a danger.

## "And they say: he is a madman" (51) — "But it is nothing but a Reminder for all the worlds" (52)

Ibn Kathir sets the two halves of the assault side by side: **they cut at him with their eyes and attack him with their tongues**, saying "he is a madman" — and they say it, he notes, *because he came with the Qur'an.* The Book that should have proved his truthfulness was the very thing they turned into evidence against him.

Ayah 52 answers in one clean sentence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: these divine words are a Reminder and an admonition for the entire universe; the Reminder lifts people from the lowest depths of degradation to the highest summits of greatness and glory, cleanses them of moral blemishes and raises their spiritual stature. So — is it possible for an insane person to receive and deliver such a sublime divine message? Can a Prophet of that calibre be called a madman?

And notice where the sūrah has arrived. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the **earlier ayat of this same sūrah rebutted the charge of insanity**, and here towards the end the same charge of lunacy is rebutted again in a different style. The sūrah is sealed at both ends against the same slander.

There is also a quiet widening in ayah 52. The taunt was thrown at one man by the people in front of him; the Book they were mocking is *dhikrun lil-ʿālamīn* — a Reminder for all the worlds.

## Living it

- **Patience is with a decree, not with a void** (48). You are waiting on something Allah has already decided and whose execution cannot be resisted. Ṣabr is the interval, not the outcome.
- **The fault being warned against is haste** (48) — Ibn Kathir's own heading for this passage. Walking off a post because results were slow and you were angry. That is what "the man of the fish" means here.
- **When you are choked with distress, pray as Yūnus did** (48): affirm Allah's oneness, declare Him free of fault, own your part. Allah's own comment on that duʿāʾ was *"And thus do We deliver the believers."*
- **The way back is open, and it goes further than repair** (49–50). His Lord did not merely release him; He *chose* him and made him one of the righteous.
- **Never look down on someone the Qur'an corrects** (50) — the Prophet ﷺ himself forbade anyone to claim to be better than Yūnus ibn Mattā.
- **Guard your own gaze** (51). When something of your brother's, or your own, or your wealth pleases you, ask Allah to bless it.
- **Take the prophetic protections** — above all the Muʿawwidhatān, which the Prophet ﷺ adopted over everything else he had used. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records from **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** that if anyone is affected by the evil eye, these two ayat (51–52) may be recited and blown over him, and the ill effect will be dispelled.
- **Let ayah 52 settle the mockery** you meet for your dīn. They called the best of creation a madman. What he brought is a Reminder for all the worlds.
